newsitem.title: USA: Jury awards Food Lion $5.5 million in ABC case.
newsitem.headline: Jury awards Food Lion $5.5 million in ABC case.

text.p: A federal jury on Wednesday ordered ABC television to pay Food Lion Inc. $5.5 million in punitive damages as a result of the network's undercover investigation of the supermarket chain.
The jury deliberated more than 30 hours over six days before reaching the decision, which also ordered two high-ranking producers for the ABC programme to pay damages totalling $45,750.
ABC, now a unit of Walt Disney Cos., said it would appeal the jury award.
The jury's decision was a victory for Food Lion, which never challenged the accuracy of ABC's 1992 report of unsanitary food handling by Food Lion workers.

The supermarket chain based in Salisbury, N.C., said ABC defrauded the company by having two journalists falsify job applications to get hired by Food Lion as a meat handler and delicatessen clerk. Once hired, the two journalists wore hidden cameras inside their clothing to videotape how Food Lion workers repackaged spoiled meat to sell to consumers.
Food Lion stock and companywide store sales plunged after the Nov. 5, 1992, broadcast.
The punitive damages came in addition to the jury's finding last month that ABC should pay $1,400 in actual damages for fraud and trespassing.

The trial was closely watched by media organisations because Food Lion, a unit of Belgian retailer Ets Delhaize Freres et Cie "LE LION" SA, chose to attack the way the story was obtained rather than file a libel lawsuit.
"The verdict of the North Carolina jury should trouble every American -- especially every journalist," ABC News President Roone Arledge said in a statement.

"After finding that the use of those undercover techniques caused Food Lion only token damages, the jury has now awarded Food Lion punitive damages of 4,000 times that amount. That result is unconscionable," Arledge said.
Lawyers for Food Lion argued the undercover journalists were employed by Food Lion and duty-bound to clean dirty meat-cutting equipment and prevent the sale of the spoiled items they filmed.
"This case was not just about money. It was about right and wrong, and the jury's first verdict was just as important to us as this decision is," said Food Lion Chairman Tom Smith.
Jurors said after the trial ended that they wanted to punish ABC for the false information given by two ABC journalists on their job applications.
"I'm not expecting every news station in the world to shut down and not be able to operate," said jury foreman Greg Mack. "But you don't have to make up information, just leave off you're with ABC."
The deliberations, lasting 30 hours over six days, were sometimes contentious. Three times, the panel sent a note to U.S. District Judge Carlton Tilley saying they were deadlocked.
Jurors said one member of the panel had argued for punitive damages as high as $1.7 billion, while another juror insisted no damages were necessary.

"We were at two extremes," said juror Tony Kinton. "A couple of jurors felt it was a large amount that needed to be involved in the punitive damages, and there was one or two of us who felt like it should be a minimum amount, if any."
Eventually the panel decided on a compromise of $5.5 million in punitive damages against the network.

The jurors also decided to order "PrimeTime Live" Executive Producer Richard Kaplan to pay $35,000, and Senior Producer Ira Rosen to pay $10,750. Food Lion lawyers suggested during closing arguments that Kaplan and Rosen be assessed $50,000 each in punitive damages.
Court documents showed that Kaplan and Rosen were paid salaries of $700,000 and $215,000, respectively, in 1993.
The jury did not assess damages against ABC journalists Lynne Dale and Susan Barnett, who worked undercover at Food Lion stores.
Barnett told reporters she hoped U.S. news organisations would continue to use undercover techniques for newsgathering.
"Investigative journalism helps people, and I hope Food Lion's legal manoeuvring doesn't scare journalists away," she said. "That would be insane."
